codeReview.summary: Solid implementation that follows existing config patterns precisely. The [queue] config section in loader.ts mirrors the sprint/budget/worktree pattern (Zod sub-schema with .default({}), CONFIG_DEFAULTS entry, ENV_MAP entries). The ProtoStep schema in proto-step.ts is well-structured with .strict() validation, EstimatedComplexity enum, and a deterministic formalizeProtoSteps() function using template-based prompt generation. The code is clean, well-documented, and the test suite is comprehensive (55 tests covering schema validation, defaults, env var overrides, boundary values, and formalization behavior). The fulfills array is correctly deep-copied to prevent mutation. All 3 modified/created files are consistent with project conventions.

issues.description: StepWithPrompt extends Step with an additional 'prompt' field, but StepSchema (in schemas.ts) uses .strict() which would reject objects with extra 'prompt' fields. If downstream code ever validates a StepWithPrompt through StepSchema.parse(), it will fail. Currently no code does this (StepSchema.parse is unused), so this is latent. Consider either adding 'prompt' as an optional field to StepSchema, or creating a StepWithPromptSchema, or documenting that StepWithPrompt must not be validated through StepSchema.

formalizeProtoSteps does not validate its input against ProtoStepSchema/ProtoStepArraySchema. The function accepts ProtoStep[] (TypeScript type) but doesn't runtime-validate. This is consistent with the rest of the codebase (validation happens at boundaries, not internal calls), but callers must ensure they pass validated data.

ProtoStepArraySchema enforces .min(1), meaning empty arrays are rejected. formalizeProtoSteps([]) would return [] without error since it doesn't validate internally. This asymmetry is fine as long as callers validate with ProtoStepArraySchema before calling formalizeProtoSteps, which the feature description implies.
